chapter: Paris 1951-70 and return to New York
title: Belgian business venture with a millionaire after de Gaulle expelled the Americans
summary: A Belgian millionaire invited Butler to open clubs after de Gaulle's order forced American forces out; the venture failed and the Paris owner complained he was not resting.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Now, then I've got an idea to have business. See, this man coming in there with pheasants and all on his back, and counting money and everything, and when he first come in to sell it." there he was as poor as he could get. "Now we're going" In the meantime I met a man called Jean Paul Lauget (PHONETIC) from Belgium. And he said, why don't you come to Belgium and let us do business. We can open up a cabaret or whatever we want to do. And he said, the Americans are going -- deGaulle and the Americans wasn't buddies then, because as I said, you cannot take them bordellos away from the Frenchmen and make them happy.

And you cannot take his wine away from him and make him happy, because that's the things he will not have you doing that there. (Inaudible) he said, we're going to stop drinking wine and drink milk. He made that statement and about six hours after that, he wasn't in there. They got him out of there immediately.

Well then, it seemed like everybody (inaudible) and deGaulle says, well, you'll have to go within the year. So the _______ now, they're going to leave because, you know, the Belgians didn't know what everybody was going to do. And what happened was he says now -- this man was a big millionaire.
He says, on your day off come over to Belgium and see what's happening. I went over there and this man had a picture of the head of John the Baptist. (Inaudible)

Yeah, and Jordan (PHONETIC), the Belgian painter (inaudible), Jordan was the man who drew it. He was a Belgian/painter, and it was beautiful. He said, I paid $200,000.00 for that, Jacques. And he had discoteques then. He had one looking like a freighter, a boat. And this ran night and day. He had 12 bartenders. Then he had another one, plush one, it ran night and day. And he says, now, we've got a thing called the Sugar Can, we can build that up again. If you come to Belgium, you've got it.

So we formed a company (inaudible). Now, I'm still working now, I'm still working at Cigale But I'm on vacation. (Inaudible). But these Americans, they're going to move in a year; they got mad and moved in a month. Pulled out, went to Belgium. Now, instead of them coming to Brussels, they went to a place called Helmut, means the helmet, about 18 miles from Brussels. Bad news. He had everything all set. And the Hilton Hotel thought that they was coming there, too. But the Hilton being rich, they could care less.
They went up there; had everything all set. So he says, Jacques (inaudible). Now, in the meantime, the owner of the place in Paris, he comes to Belgium and he says, Jacques, you

said you were going to rest. I said, yeah, I'm resting here, you see, I'm not playing no horn. "But you are running this surprised." "I know you're." I said, well, don't be surprised. Don't you realize (inaudible) business there (inaudible). He says, oh, I don't know. We can't go on like this. I said, well, I'm going to go back to my job, I'm coming back to my job on the 1st of November--Oktoberfest) season. "Oh, I don't know. I don't know." I says, well, think it over, man.
